![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14037063/assets/08ce8625dcad742776846497c4e49b5686a893be85ff1bd5426df8f8b9ce882b.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(1,1)$ and lies on both $y=f(x)$ and $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A\,(1,1)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(1)=1.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(1)=-2.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(4,2)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(2,4)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(2,4)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(2)=4.$ 
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [1,5]$ is $1$, hence, ${f}^{′}(4)=1.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is 

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{2}+{2}^{x}$ and the point $P(0,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(1,0)$ is$\,${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2}+{2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2x+{2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+2x+1.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(1).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(1)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ {x}^{3}+2x+1 & =1 \\ x({x}^{2}+2) & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(1)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+2x+1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+2 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\cdot 0+2 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{x+10}{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(4).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(4)=x.$ For $x\ne -1,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(4) & =x \\ f(x) & =4 \\ \frac{x+10}{x+1} & =4 \\ \frac{x+10}{x+1}\cdot (x+1) & =4\cdot (x+1) \\ \frac{x+10}{\cancel{(x+1)}}\cdot \cancel{(x+1)} & =4x+4 \\ x+10 & =4x+4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(4)=2.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+10}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{9}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{9}{{(2+1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{(3)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{9} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=1+2{e}^{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(3).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(3)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(3) & =x \\ f(x) & =3 \\ 1+2{e}^{x+1} & =3 \\ 2{e}^{x+1} & =2 \\ {e}^{x+1} & =1 \\ x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(3)=-1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(-1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =1+2{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =2{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x).
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1) =\dfrac{g(1)}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}+g'(1)f^{-1}(1).
$$

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(1)=2,$ $g(1)=-3,$ $g'(1)=1,$ and $f'(2)=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}\cdot g)^{′}(1) & =\frac{g(1)}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}+{g}^{′}(1){f}^{-1}(1) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{f}^{′}(2)}+1\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-3}{-1}+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) =3e^{x}-1.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x}-1 & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) = 0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{e}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
